That is a count. Divide it by the 214 in AAA.
That divides by the 109 in BBB, so it is P(A∣B)P(A \mid B)P(A∣B). Given AAA, divide by the 214 in AAA.

That is P(B)P(B)P(B), which ignores the condition.
Given AAA: look only at the column for AAA, and its total.
P(B∣A)=∣A∩B∣/∣A∣P(B \mid A) = |A \cap B| / |A|P(B∣A)=∣A∩B∣/∣A∣.

9b apply Bayes' rule, with natural frequencies, and explain the base-rate effect.

Your answerBayes' rule, and natural frequencies out of 10 0009b

HHH: the payment is fraudulent. EEE: the system flags it. For a payment picked at random, P(H)=0.01P(H) = 0.01P(H)=0.01, P(E∣H)=0.9P(E \mid H) = 0.9P(E∣H)=0.9 and P(E∣Hc)=0.05P(E \mid H^c) = 0.05P(E∣Hc)=0.05. What is P(H∣E)P(H \mid E)P(H∣E), the probability that the payment is fraudulent, given that the system flags it? Give 3 decimal places.

That is P(E∣H)P(E \mid H)P(E∣H), the sensitivity. Bayes' rule turns it round: P(H∣E)=P(E∣H)P(H)/P(E)P(H \mid E) = P(E \mid H)P(H)/P(E)P(H∣E)=P(E∣H)P(H)/P(E).
That is the prior, P(H)P(H)P(H), before the evidence. The evidence EEE changes it.
That is the specificity, P(Ec∣Hc)P(E^c \mid H^c)P(Ec∣Hc): the chance a negative case is cleared.
That is P(H∩E)P(H \cap E)P(H∩E), the numerator only. Divide by P(E)P(E)P(E), all the ways to get EEE.
That is P(E)P(E)P(E), the denominator. Bayes' rule divides P(E∣H)P(H)P(E \mid H)P(H)P(E∣H)P(H) by it.
That is P(Hc∣E)P(H^c \mid E)P(Hc∣E), the chance that EEE is a false alarm.
Think of 10 000: how many have HHH and EEE, and how many have EEE without HHH?
P(H∣E)=P(E∣H)P(H)P(E∣H)P(H)+P(E∣Hc)P(Hc)P(H \mid E) = \dfrac{P(E \mid H)P(H)}{P(E \mid H)P(H) + P(E \mid H^c)P(H^c)}P(H∣E)=P(E∣H)P(H)+P(E∣Hc)P(Hc)P(E∣H)P(H)​.
Solution

P(E)=0.9×0.01+0.05×0.99=0.0585P(E) = 0.9 \times 0.01 + 0.05 \times 0.99 = 0.0585P(E)=0.9×0.01+0.05×0.99=0.0585, so P(H∣E)=0.009/0.0585≈0.154P(H \mid E) = 0.009/0.0585 \approx 0.154P(H∣E)=0.009/0.0585≈0.154. As natural frequencies: out of 10 000, 90 have EEE with HHH and 495 without, so 90/585≈0.15490/585 \approx 0.15490/585≈0.154.

ChooseThe base-rate effect: why a positive is often a false alarm9b

The same test is used in two groups. In group 1, 0.5% of the bags at an airport hold a banned item. In group 2, 2% of the bags at an airport hold a banned item. In both groups, the scanner raises an alert for 95% of these bags and for 2% of the others. HHH: the bag holds a banned item. EEE: the scanner raises an alert. One from each group gets EEE. For which one is HHH more likely?

The one from group 2
Right: P(H∣E)≈0.193P(H \mid E) \approx 0.193P(H∣E)≈0.193 in group 1 and 0.4920.4920.492 in group 2. The same evidence, a larger prior, a larger posterior.
The one from group 1
The prior matters: P(H)P(H)P(H) is 0.5% there, the smaller one, so a positive is more often a false alarm.
Equally likely: the test is the same in both groups
The test's rates are the same, but P(H∣E)P(H \mid E)P(H∣E) also depends on the prior, P(H)P(H)P(H): the base rate.
You cannot tell without the number in each group
Bayes' rule needs only the shares: the prior, the sensitivity and the false-positive rate.

LinkNo linkTotalSpam431255Not spam7142149Total50154204\begin{array}{l|cc|c} & \text{Link} & \text{No link} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Spam} & 43 & 12 & 55 \\ \text{Not spam} & 7 & 142 & 149 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 50 & 154 & 204 \end{array}SpamNot spamTotal​Link43750​No link12142154​Total55149204​​

Somewhere else the class shares are Spam 0.2, Not spam 0.8, but within each class the share with EEE is the same as in the table. A email from there shows EEE. What is P(Spam∣E)P(\text{Spam} \mid E)P(Spam∣E) there? Give 3 decimal places.

That uses the table's own class shares as the prior. The new place has a different prior.
That is the likelihood, P(E∣Spam)P(E \mid \text{Spam})P(E∣Spam), not the posterior.

That is the new prior, before the evidence.

The prior is the new shares. Posterior = prior × likelihood, divided by its sum.

9b apply Bayes' rule, with natural frequencies, and explain the base-rate effect.

Your answerBayes' rule, and natural frequencies out of 10 0009b

2% of the people screened have the disease. The test is positive for 85% of people with the disease and negative for 92% of people without it. Pick one at random. HHH: the person has the disease. EEE: the test is positive. What is P(H∣E)P(H \mid E)P(H∣E), the probability that the person has the disease, given that the test is positive? Give 3 decimal places.

That is P(E∣H)P(E \mid H)P(E∣H), the sensitivity. Bayes' rule turns it round: P(H∣E)=P(E∣H)P(H)/P(E)P(H \mid E) = P(E \mid H)P(H)/P(E)P(H∣E)=P(E∣H)P(H)/P(E).
That is the prior, P(H)P(H)P(H), before the evidence. The evidence EEE changes it.
That is the specificity, P(Ec∣Hc)P(E^c \mid H^c)P(Ec∣Hc): the chance a negative case is cleared.
That is P(H∩E)P(H \cap E)P(H∩E), the numerator only. Divide by P(E)P(E)P(E), all the ways to get EEE.
That is P(E)P(E)P(E), the denominator. Bayes' rule divides P(E∣H)P(H)P(E \mid H)P(H)P(E∣H)P(H) by it.

prior holds P(class)P(\text{class})P(class) and like holds P(E∣class)P(E \mid \text{class})P(E∣class) for the classes Apple, Pear, Orange. Which expression gives the posterior vector, P(class∣E)P(\text{class} \mid E)P(class∣E) for every class?

import numpy as np

# Apple, Pear, Orange
prior = np.array([0.2, 0.15, 0.65])
like = np.array([0.7, 0.9, 0.75])    # P(E | class), E: the fruit weighs over 150 g
prior * like / np.sum(prior * like)
Right: prior × likelihood for each class, divided by its sum, P(E)P(E)P(E), so the posterior adds up to 1.
like / like.sum()
That normalises the likelihoods alone and forgets the prior.
prior @ like
That is one number, P(E)P(E)P(E): the denominator of Bayes' rule, not the posterior vector.
(prior + like) / (prior + like).sum()
Bayes multiplies the prior by the likelihood; it does not add them.
Choose9b

A customer shows E1E_1E1​ and then E2E_2E2​, which are independent within each class. post1 is the posterior after E1E_1E1​. Which expression gives the posterior after both?

import numpy as np

# New, Returning
prior = np.array([0.75, 0.25])
like1 = np.array([0.5, 0.6])    # P(E1 | class), E1: the customer uses a discount code
like2 = np.array([0.85, 0.75])    # P(E2 | class), E2: the customer shops on a phone

post1 = prior * like1 / (prior * like1).sum()
prior * like1 * like2 / (prior * like1 * like2).sum()
Right: yesterday's posterior is today's prior. Multiply by the new likelihood and divide by the sum.
post1 * like2
That is not divided by its sum: the entries don't add up to 1.
(post1 + like2) / (post1 + like2).sum()
Bayes multiplies by the likelihood; it does not add.
post1 * like2 / like2.sum()
Divide by the sum of post1 * like2, not of the likelihoods.
